Oakland: eScholarship / California Digital Library (open access, CC-BY), 628 pp. https://escholarship.org/uc/item/5zx6z32d. Chapter 5 'Tone' (family-wide prosody statement, §1; Miya terraced-level tone system, §4.3, summarising Schuh 1998, A Grammar of Miya, UC Publications in Linguistics 130, Chapter 3) and Chapter 1 §4 'Original Book Outline'.
catalog_locator: Ch. 5 'Tone' §1 Introduction, printed p. 89 = PDF p. 108; Ch. 1 §4 'Original Book Outline', item 5 'Tones and Intonation', printed p. 6 = PDF p. 25; Miya tone system Ch. 5 §4.3 'Terraced level tone systems', printed pp. 124-126 = PDF pp. 143-145. Saved file: the copy we hold (628 pp., text layer), re-opened with during this reading.
catalog_quote: p. 89: "Chadic languages make use of three prosodic properties: tone, intonation, and syllable weight. All Chadic languages are tone languages, i.e. relative voice pitch on individual syllables is part of the lexical representation of words and has the potential for making morphosyntactic distinctions. ... Syllable weight, usually typified by a contrast between long and short vowels, is an important prosodic property of many—probably a large majority—of Chadic languages. Stress as distinctive prosodic property has been discussed in Hunter (1980) for Hausa and Wolff (1983, 2015b) for Lamang (and perhaps in a few other Chadic language studies), but prosodic amplitude in Chadic phonological systems generally is a function of the interaction of tone, syllable weight, and intonation and plays no role that is not attributable to those properties." p. 6 (book outline, item 5 Tones and Intonation): "- stress: no Chadic language has stress as a prosodic parameter". p. 124: "A good example from West Chadic is the North Bauchi language Miya (I.B.2.a). Here, I give only some of the basic features of the Miya system. Schuh (1998:Chapter 3) provides a fuller, detailed description. ... Tonal domains have three possible lexical specifications, called Toneless (T), High (H), and Low (L) in Schuh (1998)."
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Miya is a tone language (terraced-level system: lexical Toneless / High / Low domains, downstepped H, L-raising; Schuh 2017 pp. 124-126 after Schuh 1998 ch. 3). The same author states for the whole Chadic family that stress is not a prosodic parameter: whatever syllable prominence exists follows from tone, syllable weight and intonation, so there is no word-stress rule to state for Miya.
new_statements.exceptions: Schuh notes that stress has been claimed as distinctive for Hausa (Hunter 1980) and Lamang (Wolff 1983, 2015b), 'and perhaps in a few other Chadic language studies', but attributes prominence in Chadic generally to tone, weight and intonation. Miya is not among the languages for which stress has been claimed.
new_statements.domain_note: The stress statement is a family-wide generalisation about Chadic, not a sentence about Miya specifically; it comes from the author of the only Miya grammar, in a book whose Miya section (pp. 124-126) treats Miya purely as a terraced-level tone language and never mentions stress. Tone description is of citation forms and phonological phrases (N+N genitives, demonstrative+N, N+numeral, verb+object). The Miya grammar itself (Schuh 1998, ch. 2-3) was not opened and may contain an explicit Miya-specific remark on stress.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the Miya of Miya town, Bauchi State (Schuh's 1982-83 fieldwork with Vaziya Ciroma Tilde Miya) = miya1266 / mkf; no dialect distinction is made. Cornucopia code 'I.B.2.a' = North Bauchi group of West Chadic. The stress statement itself is scoped to the whole Chadic family, not to Miya alone.
